<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:attribution-sets" data-paper-title="Statistical Learning from Attribution Sets" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Learning signals, multitask learning, and feedback bias</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-attribution-sets-5c9ffe92" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-47a34e025140d9eb">What do Attribution Sets reveal and what do they leave unspecified?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aattribution-sets">Statistical Learning from Attribution Sets</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google Research</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>They constrain which clicks may be linked to a conversion, but provide no unique true match; different sets can overlap. Set statistics can support risk estimation, not a definitive label for each click. Keep that distinction separate from true individual attribution.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Knowing that a purchase could follow any of three impressions does not justify labeling all three as positives or arbitrarily choosing one.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.06276">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../recommendation-components/2602.06276-attribution-sets/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-47a34e025140d9eb">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:attribution-sets" data-paper-title="Statistical Learning from Attribution Sets" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Learning signals, multitask learning, and feedback bias</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-ae6528b34b9ff368">Why not randomly label one click positive when the conversion attribution is only known as a set?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aattribution-sets">Statistical Learning from Attribution Sets</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google Research</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Random pairing invents a precise label, and overlapping sets can affect the same event repeatedly. The method splits binary loss into a label-independent term and a label-dependent moment, estimating risk from set statistics without fabricating individual matches. The printed coefficient for multi-element sets failed a local constant-function check, so the counterexample is retained and the estimator is not fully validated.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Three impressions may be associated with a purchase and two may also appear in a different attribution set. Choosing one arbitrarily changes the supervision; set statistics also need consistency checks.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.06276">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../recommendation-components/2602.06276-attribution-sets/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-ae6528b34b9ff368">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:attribution-sets" data-paper-title="Statistical Learning from Attribution Sets" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Learning signals, multitask learning, and feedback bias</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-32641f7c8cf39a07">How do the assumptions of Attribution Sets risk decomposition differ from maximum-prior pseudo-labeling?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aattribution-sets">Statistical Learning from Attribution Sets</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google Research</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Pseudo-labeling chooses a hidden match before training as if it had full supervision. Risk decomposition keeps the match unidentifiable and uses population moments and a position prior for the label-dependent term. It avoids claiming individual ground truth, but still requires a valid estimator and inputs. The local counterexample is a limited check of the printed coefficient, not a corrected replacement theory.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A prior that favors the first impression does not make it the true positive. If the set estimator fails the constant-function check, audit it rather than reporting an unbiased result.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.06276">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../recommendation-components/2602.06276-attribution-sets/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-32641f7c8cf39a07">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:attribution-sets" data-paper-title="Statistical Learning from Attribution Sets" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Learning signals, multitask learning, and feedback bias</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-c450c5f39527fd2b">Why must an Attribution Sets implementation not silently clip singular denominators or renormalize by the window count?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aattribution-sets">Statistical Learning from Attribution Sets</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google Research</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The binomial tail probability, selection indicator, and fixed denominator together define the paper&#x27;s estimator. Changing the denominator changes the statistical object. Fail explicitly at singular boundaries and distinguish known population moments from sample plug-in estimates. Keep the multi-element counterexample visible rather than masking it with a numerical fallback.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Replacing a zero denominator with a tiny positive number returns a finite result but not the paper&#x27;s estimator. Report that its assumptions do not hold for that input.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.06276">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../recommendation-components/2602.06276-attribution-sets/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-c450c5f39527fd2b">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:baff" data-paper-title="BAFF: Bid-Aware Filter Family for Mitigating Training Data Interference in RTB A/B Tests" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Learning signals, multitask learning, and feedback bias</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-baff-e8ac8fd9" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-213d144919ea826f">Why does treatment interference arise in the RTB A/B logs studied by BAFF?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Abaff">BAFF: Bid-Aware Filter Family for Mitigating Training Data Interference in RTB A/B Tests</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Dable</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Policy choices affect bidding opportunities and prices. An ad decision in one arm may change the competition the other policy actually faces, so A&#x27;s logs are not automatically examples of what B would observe. Filtering approximately interference-free cases limits transfer; it does not make the arm labels interchangeable.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>When A raises an ad&#x27;s bid, it can alter the competition. B may not have won the same opportunity at the same price, so treating the record as ordinary B training data imports A&#x27;s policy effect.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.08725">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2609.08725-baff/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-213d144919ea826f">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:baff" data-paper-title="BAFF: Bid-Aware Filter Family for Mitigating Training Data Interference in RTB A/B Tests" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Learning signals, multitask learning, and feedback bias</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-14b2794811c5695a">Why does BAFF check both rank and bid-price differences?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Abaff">BAFF: Bid-Aware Filter Family for Mitigating Training Data Interference in RTB A/B Tests</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Dable</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Similar ranks can still imply different win probabilities if bids differ; similar bids can still produce different exposure when ranks move. The two conditions remove A logs likely to affect policy B&#x27;s decisions and reduce training interference. Retained samples are more transferable under these conditions, not evidence of a truly interference-free market.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A similarly ranked ad may win because A bids much higher. Conversely, equal bids do not make logs interchangeable if a rank crosses the display boundary.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.08725">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2609.08725-baff/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-14b2794811c5695a">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:baff" data-paper-title="BAFF: Bid-Aware Filter Family for Mitigating Training Data Interference in RTB A/B Tests" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Learning signals, multitask learning, and feedback bias</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-4ec25e619cf3dc9a">How does BAFF&#x27;s filtering differ from uniformly downweighting all A logs?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Abaff">BAFF: Bid-Aware Filter Family for Mitigating Training Data Interference in RTB A/B Tests</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Dable</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Uniform downweighting preserves all samples, including opportunities severely affected by A. The two-condition filter rejects incompatible logs based on rank position under B and the bid difference. This can reduce interference at the cost of sample count; stricter thresholds are not always better and do not ensure unbiased survivors.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Halving the weight of a log with similar prices but very different ranks still uses it. Filtering rejects it, but an overly strict filter can leave too little data and raise variance.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.08725">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2609.08725-baff/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-4ec25e619cf3dc9a">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:baff" data-paper-title="BAFF: Bid-Aware Filter Family for Mitigating Training Data Interference in RTB A/B Tests" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Learning signals, multitask learning, and feedback bias</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-1a6ce48b374de43a">Why does BAFF&#x27;s bid-price distance count only the positive excess of A over B?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Abaff">BAFF: Bid-Aware Filter Family for Mitigating Training Data Interference in RTB A/B Tests</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Dable</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The paper uses `max(bpA−bpB,0)/bpA`, which measures upward price movement in that direction, not a symmetric absolute gap. Rank distance is the position in B divided by K. Keep the direction, normalization, and two separate thresholds.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A bid of 10 versus B&#x27;s 8 yields 20%; A&#x27;s 8 versus B&#x27;s 10 does not yield the same positive penalty. An absolute difference would change the filter.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.08725">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2609.08725-baff/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-1a6ce48b374de43a">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:baseline-incremental" data-paper-title="Baseline and Incremental: User, Item, and Request Debiasing in Instagram Feed Ranking" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Learning signals, multitask learning, and feedback bias</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-baseline-incremental-a452c157" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-92981c6733d15b6c">What reference points do the user, item, and request baselines represent in Baseline-Incremental?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Abaseline-incremental">Baseline and Incremental: User, Item, and Request Debiasing in Instagram Feed Ranking</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Meta</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The user baseline captures customary response, the item baseline broad attractiveness, and the request baseline the current candidate pool&#x27;s level. Increment scores show how a candidate stands out; raw scores keep absolute value. This is not causal uplift, and a different reference changes the ranking&#x27;s meaning.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A high-activity user&#x27;s video click probability may only slightly exceed their norm, whereas a moderate probability for a less active user is more exceptional. Retain both absolute values.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.27423v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../recommendation-components/2610.27423-baseline-incremental/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-92981c6733d15b6c">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:baseline-incremental" data-paper-title="Baseline and Incremental: User, Item, and Request Debiasing in Instagram Feed Ranking" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Learning signals, multitask learning, and feedback bias</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-047a61e14691f63d">Why keep the raw prediction after subtracting a user or item baseline?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Abaseline-incremental">Baseline and Incremental: User, Item, and Request Debiasing in Instagram Feed Ranking</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Meta</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The increment measures how far above normal a candidate is, while the raw score preserves absolute business magnitude. The method separately weights a nonlinear increment: compare probabilities in log-odds space and use same-unit differences for regressions. This is a scoring configuration, not causal uplift.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A small lift over a low baseline can outrank a more valuable candidate on relative change alone; the raw score keeps the high baseline&#x27;s value visible.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.27423v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../recommendation-components/2610.27423-baseline-incremental/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-047a61e14691f63d">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:baseline-incremental" data-paper-title="Baseline and Incremental: User, Item, and Request Debiasing in Instagram Feed Ranking" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Learning signals, multitask learning, and feedback bias</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-ca6aded4d44a4977">Why use log-odds differences for probabilities but original-unit differences for regression?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Abaseline-incremental">Baseline and Incremental: User, Item, and Request Debiasing in Instagram Feed Ranking</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Meta</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>An equal absolute probability difference has a different meaning near zero or one; logit differences express change on the odds scale. Regression targets already have natural units. These distinct scoring responses are intentional and do not confer a causal interpretation.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Click-through rates of 1% to 2% and 40% to 41% both gain one point but change odds differently; extra watch time can be compared directly in seconds.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.27423v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../recommendation-components/2610.27423-baseline-incremental/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-ca6aded4d44a4977">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:baseline-incremental" data-paper-title="Baseline and Incremental: User, Item, and Request Debiasing in Instagram Feed Ranking" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Learning signals, multitask learning, and feedback bias</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-ed719753753ebfda">Why not implement Baseline-Incremental&#x27;s demotion gate as the negative of its promotion gate?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Abaseline-incremental">Baseline and Incremental: User, Item, and Request Debiasing in Instagram Feed Ranking</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Meta</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>When the promotion amplitude is prediction p, it naturally vanishes near zero. Negating it would barely penalize the low-p candidates that most need demotion. Preserve the constant and gap amplitudes and piecewise limits from the source, explicitly clip probabilities before taking logits, and verify the gates separately.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A candidate with p near zero receives almost no penalty from −p, while constant demotion can still suppress it.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.27423v1">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../recommendation-components/2610.27423-baseline-incremental/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-ed719753753ebfda">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:casi" data-paper-title="CASI: Credit Assignment via Set Intervention for Agentic Retrieval" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Learning signals, multitask learning, and feedback bias</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-casi-2c2b2f1b" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-807a571ed774579f">Why does CASI separate one retrieval per action from re-evaluation of subsets?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Acasi">CASI: Credit Assignment via Set Intervention for Agentic Retrieval</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Xiaohongshu</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Reretrieval can change action results across subsets, mixing backend randomness with cooperation effects. Freeze action candidate snapshots first and then recombine them to compare marginal contributions over identical evidence. State assumptions about evaluation backend sensitivity.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Removing one of two equivalent queries may leave the set unchanged. If reretrieval changes the results, redundancy and retrieval fluctuation are no longer distinguishable.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.20293">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2610.20293-casi/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-807a571ed774579f">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:casi" data-paper-title="CASI: Credit Assignment via Set Intervention for Agentic Retrieval" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Learning signals, multitask learning, and feedback bias</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-26fe8a4e5a7b2ef3">Why does CASI freeze retrieval snapshots and recombine subsets rather than split the set reward evenly?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Acasi">CASI: Credit Assignment via Set Intervention for Agentic Retrieval</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Xiaohongshu</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Actions can complement or substitute for each other. CASI retrieves once per action, computes marginal value across subsets of fixed results, and shapes advantages with Shapley credit. This avoids repeated-retrieval noise but does not establish an identical unbiased gradient to the original set objective.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>If rewrites A and B retrieve the same products and C adds a new category, averaging overstates redundant actions; fixed-set recombination exposes C&#x27;s contribution.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.20293">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2610.20293-casi/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-26fe8a4e5a7b2ef3">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:casi" data-paper-title="CASI: Credit Assignment via Set Intervention for Agentic Retrieval" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Learning signals, multitask learning, and feedback bias</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-b413a4921e7951f0">Why are Singleton and LOO generally insufficient to recover CASI&#x27;s Shapley credit with four or more actions?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Acasi">CASI: Credit Assignment via Set Intervention for Agentic Retrieval</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Xiaohongshu</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Singleton observes individual values and leave-one-out observes removal from the full set. Shapley averages marginal contributions across all coalitions, including intermediate subsets with higher-order cooperation. Equal endpoint values do not fix intermediate values; additive cases need no extra intervention.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Two queries may be useless alone but jointly cover a need, and a third can replace one. Singles or full-set removals can miss the dependency.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.20293">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2610.20293-casi/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-b413a4921e7951f0">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:casi" data-paper-title="CASI: Credit Assignment via Set Intervention for Agentic Retrieval" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Learning signals, multitask learning, and feedback bias</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-beb70d44bd05caec">Why jointly project CASI&#x27;s bounded zero-sum advantages instead of clipping dimensions independently?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Acasi">CASI: Credit Assignment via Set Intervention for Agentic Retrieval</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Xiaohongshu</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Independent clipping breaks zero sum and can shift the mean action advantage away from the original rollout advantage. Joint projection solves for a shared offset λ before clipping to satisfy both bounds and zero sum. It preserves the arithmetic action mean, not a token-length-weighted mean, and does not guarantee the original unbiased gradient.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Clipping (2, −1, −1) to ±1 yields a negative sum. A common offset before clipping can meet both constraints.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.20293">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2610.20293-casi/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-beb70d44bd05caec">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:causal-representation" data-paper-title="Causal Representation Learning for Generalisable Recommendation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Learning signals, multitask learning, and feedback bias</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-causal-representation-dd23e0e4" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-003a7305ed9c5c96">Why does Causal Representation both retain outcome information and suppress confounding information?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Acausal-representation">Causal Representation Learning for Generalisable Recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Warwick</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Suppressing exposure information alone can remove genuine preference; preserving outcome prediction alone can exploit exposure shortcuts. The dual objective uses conditional outcome information and a confounding penalty to retain generalizable signals. These constraints do not establish causal identification without variable and data assumptions.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Removing popularity entirely can lose demand information; keeping it unconditionally can copy the old exposure policy.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.27043">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2605.27043-causal-representation/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-003a7305ed9c5c96">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:causal-representation" data-paper-title="Causal Representation Learning for Generalisable Recommendation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Learning signals, multitask learning, and feedback bias</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-ad3fba55e7e132de">Why does deleting all exposure-related information not necessarily produce a good causal recommendation representation?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Acausal-representation">Causal Representation Learning for Generalisable Recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Warwick</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Some signals relate to both exposure and real outcomes. The information-theoretic objective balances outcome information conditional on confounders against dependence on exposure, aiming to preserve transferable information. Causal interpretation still depends on confounders and identification assumptions; distribution-shift metrics alone do not prove all noncausal information was removed.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Geography affects both exposure and delivery feasibility. Distinguish targeting preference from real delivery effects instead of deleting every regional signal.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.27043">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2605.27043-causal-representation/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-ad3fba55e7e132de">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:causal-representation" data-paper-title="Causal Representation Learning for Generalisable Recommendation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Learning signals, multitask learning, and feedback bias</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-4f562272774bfd8f">Where do causal representation constraints act compared with IPS weighting?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Acausal-representation">Causal Representation Learning for Generalisable Recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Warwick</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Representation constraints change what the encoder stores, while IPS changes how much observed samples contribute to loss. The former needs confounder representations and information estimates; the latter needs valid propensities and support. Proxy results do not establish that one is generally better.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Weighting rare impressions does not stop the model reading popularity. Suppressing popularity does not create missing unexposed samples.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.27043">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2605.27043-causal-representation/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-4f562272774bfd8f">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:causal-representation" data-paper-title="Causal Representation Learning for Generalisable Recommendation" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Learning signals, multitask learning, and feedback bias</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-dcd516fbb0b0b066">How can an implementation of `I(g(T);Y|Z)−λI(g(T);Z)` avoid using target labels at serving time?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Acausal-representation">Causal Representation Learning for Generalisable Recommendation</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · University of Warwick</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Y and Z can enter the training objective and estimator; the deployed representation must be computed solely from T available at prediction. The source reports no extra serving overhead after training, but the local public proxy does not prove that causal components were separated.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Use clicks to train g(T), then compute it before the current click occurs. Concatenating the observed click at serving would leak the answer.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.27043">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2605.27043-causal-representation/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-dcd516fbb0b0b066">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:causal-retrieval" data-paper-title="Deep-learning Causal Retrieval Optimization for Efficient e-commerce Distribution in Pinterest" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Learning signals, multitask learning, and feedback bias</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-causal-retrieval-c13802af" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-dd18e3e23c61a9ea">What are the treatment and outcome in causal retrieval?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Acausal-retrieval">Deep-learning Causal Retrieval Optimization for Efficient e-commerce Distribution in Pinterest</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Pinterest</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Treatment is whether the shopping candidate generator runs; outcomes are later business responses across events. Estimate the trigger/no-trigger difference for comparable users, not ordinary shopping-model accuracy. Both decisions must be sufficiently represented in the data.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>The question is whether running shopping retrieval changes purchase or consumption for the same context, not whether that user likes to shop anyway.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14161">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2607.14161-causal-retrieval/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-dd18e3e23c61a9ea">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:causal-retrieval" data-paper-title="Deep-learning Causal Retrieval Optimization for Efficient e-commerce Distribution in Pinterest" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Learning signals, multitask learning, and feedback bias</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-188923aec4e8da1a">Why decide whether to trigger causal retrieval by uplift instead of underlying shopping probability?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Acausal-retrieval">Deep-learning Causal Retrieval Optimization for Efficient e-commerce Distribution in Pinterest</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Pinterest</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>High-propensity users might buy without retrieval, so allocate compute by the outcome changed by triggering. Use randomized logs to learn treated and control outcomes, doubly robust correction to estimate increment, and replay to select a threshold. Adequate experimental support and overlap are still necessary.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A likely buyer may gain little, while a less likely buyer can be persuaded by relevant candidates. Under a budget, compare intervention increments rather than base propensity.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14161">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2607.14161-causal-retrieval/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-188923aec4e8da1a">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:causal-retrieval" data-paper-title="Deep-learning Causal Retrieval Optimization for Efficient e-commerce Distribution in Pinterest" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Learning signals, multitask learning, and feedback bias</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-8b7a2a15a35fac28">What does DR uplift add beyond two outcome models for treatment and control?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Acausal-retrieval">Deep-learning Causal Retrieval Optimization for Efficient e-commerce Distribution in Pinterest</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Pinterest</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The model difference estimates the outcome gap; a propensity-weighted residual uses observed assignment information to correct fitting error. Double robustness depends on its assumptions and suitable model specification, not immunity to arbitrary bias. Local synthetic randomized treatments do not establish production uplift.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>The residual may correct underestimated treated purchases, but cannot fix zero support when this group has never received treatment.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14161">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2607.14161-causal-retrieval/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-8b7a2a15a35fac28">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:causal-retrieval" data-paper-title="Deep-learning Causal Retrieval Optimization for Efficient e-commerce Distribution in Pinterest" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Learning signals, multitask learning, and feedback bias</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-edf0a7c6fee81043">Why check propensity values near zero or one in causal retrieval?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Acausal-retrieval">Deep-learning Causal Retrieval Optimization for Efficient e-commerce Distribution in Pinterest</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Pinterest</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The DR residuals divide by e(x) or 1−e(x); extremes amplify noise, and missing overlap can prevent estimation. Choose trigger thresholds on independent replay or validation rather than test. Document any clipping because it changes estimator bias and variance.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A subgroup triggered only 1% of the time can give one outcome enormous weight; a high score caused by that denominator is not high-confidence uplift.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.14161">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2607.14161-causal-retrieval/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-edf0a7c6fee81043">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:click-a-buy-b" data-paper-title="Click A, Buy B: Rethinking Conversion Attribution in E-Commerce Recommendations" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Learning signals, multitask learning, and feedback bias</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-click-a-buy-b-aac757e9" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-fba99f94af149fd0">Why does Click-A-Buy-B distinguish clicked and purchased items?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aclick-a-buy-b">Click A, Buy B: Rethinking Conversion Attribution in E-Commerce Recommendations</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Pinterest</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>An item can reveal a need and another item satisfy it through price or specs. Separate CABA and CABB supervision retains direct conversions and cross-item guidance; taxonomy offers relation cues. Observed co-occurrence does not prove that A causes purchase of B.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Clicking one camera brand and buying another is not a conversion of A, but A can still participate in the decision.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.15113">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2507.15113-click-a-buy-b/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-fba99f94af149fd0">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:click-a-buy-b" data-paper-title="Click A, Buy B: Rethinking Conversion Attribution in E-Commerce Recommendations" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Learning signals, multitask learning, and feedback bias</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-fb5e3facbeeba7ab">Why not attribute a purchase of B entirely to clicked item A as a conversion of A itself?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aclick-a-buy-b">Click A, Buy B: Rethinking Conversion Attribution in E-Commerce Recommendations</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Pinterest</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The clicked and purchased objects can differ; same-item last-click attribution misses cross-item paths. Separate Click-A-Buy-A and Click-A-Buy-B tasks and use taxonomy to describe relations between A and B. This improves observed attribution and prediction, not causal identification.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A user views an entry-level camera and buys an upgrade. Same-item counting marks the first camera as worthless despite its role in the decision path.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.15113">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2507.15113-click-a-buy-b/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-fb5e3facbeeba7ab">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:click-a-buy-b" data-paper-title="Click A, Buy B: Rethinking Conversion Attribution in E-Commerce Recommendations" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Learning signals, multitask learning, and feedback bias</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-006455c4de387e4b">Why does CABB need behavior types and item hierarchy beyond ordinary next-item prediction?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aclick-a-buy-b">Click A, Buy B: Rethinking Conversion Attribution in E-Commerce Recommendations</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Pinterest</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Adjacency alone need not distinguish browsing, clicking, and purchase or describe the A–B relationship. CABB explicitly supervises cross-item purchase paths and uses taxonomy to organize transferable relations. Sequential viewing preserves adjacency only and does not validate real purchase attribution.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Watching movie B after A can test cross-item connections, but there is no ad-click and transaction loop.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.15113">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2507.15113-click-a-buy-b/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-006455c4de387e4b">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:click-a-buy-b" data-paper-title="Click A, Buy B: Rethinking Conversion Attribution in E-Commerce Recommendations" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Learning signals, multitask learning, and feedback bias</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-2cc0afb634ea21f7">How should a CABB viewing-sequence proxy be reported without inventing purchase labels?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Aclick-a-buy-b">Click A, Buy B: Rethinking Conversion Attribution in E-Commerce Recommendations</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Pinterest</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>State that sequential views proxy Click-A/Buy-B, compare matched data, candidates, and baselines, and limit conclusions to the proxy. Taxonomy weights connect corresponding items and must not use test targets to decide candidate categories. Public ratings are not transaction amounts.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Report simulated cross-item paths from successive views, not that users really clicked A and bought B. A target category known only afterward is not an inference input.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 本地复现. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.15113">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2507.15113-click-a-buy-b/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-2cc0afb634ea21f7">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:cross-task-relationships" data-paper-title="Learned Cross-Task Relationships in Multi-Task Models" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Learning signals, multitask learning, and feedback bias</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-cross-task-relationships-c0c2f1d1" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-992bd51e3399c8a0">Why can multitask models with the same marginals predict different joint behavior?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Across-task-relationships">Learned Cross-Task Relationships in Multi-Task Models</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Marginals give frequencies, not co-occurrence. Covariance is joint probability minus the product of marginals, adding dependence information to shared representations and decisions. The task pair needs enough nondegenerate combinations; mutually exclusive or constant labels do not support the same interpretation.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Click and long-watch can each have probability one half while always coinciding or never coinciding.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.28776">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../recommendation-components/2609.28776-cross-task-relationships/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-992bd51e3399c8a0">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:cross-task-relationships" data-paper-title="Learned Cross-Task Relationships in Multi-Task Models" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Learning signals, multitask learning, and feedback bias</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-3a67c9b61c5a23fb">Why predict a joint like-and-click label when both marginal rates are already predicted?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Across-task-relationships">Learned Cross-Task Relationships in Multi-Task Models</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Marginals do not determine whether feedback occurs on the same examples. A joint head models dependence for shared representation supervision and downstream decisions; validate the benefits separately. Check feasibility when reconstructing the distribution rather than clipping negative probabilities and claiming calibration.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Both rates can be 20% with complete overlap or complete separation. Marginals alone cannot tell how to combine objectives.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.28776">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../recommendation-components/2609.28776-cross-task-relationships/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-3a67c9b61c5a23fb">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:cross-task-relationships" data-paper-title="Learned Cross-Task Relationships in Multi-Task Models" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Learning signals, multitask learning, and feedback bias</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-406fe847530f0af1">Why compare true cross-label auxiliary supervision with shuffled labels rather than only adding or removing parameters?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Across-task-relationships">Learned Cross-Task Relationships in Multi-Task Models</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>An extra head can change the backbone through more gradients or regularization. Shuffling keeps the training form while destroying real task relations, helping isolate the relation signal. A sparse small slice is still only diagnostic and does not support stable capability claims.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>If real click-and-long-watch labels help but equal-sized shuffled labels do not, that supports useful joint information; similar results may reflect auxiliary training alone.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.28776">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../recommendation-components/2609.28776-cross-task-relationships/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-406fe847530f0af1">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:cross-task-relationships" data-paper-title="Learned Cross-Task Relationships in Multi-Task Models" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Learning signals, multitask learning, and feedback bias</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-a3d34d2a90b174f4">Why not silently clip negative probabilities when reconstructing four joint cells from pX, pY, and pXY?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Across-task-relationships">Learned Cross-Task Relationships in Multi-Task Models</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Google</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The cells must be nonnegative and sum to one; pXY is also bounded by the marginals. Negatives expose inconsistent predictions. Preserve an infeasible marker instead of clipping and claiming calibration; observed labels belong in loss and evaluation, not pre-impression inputs.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>pX=0.2 and pXY=0.4 imply negative click-only probability, which should be reported as inconsistent.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.28776">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../recommendation-components/2609.28776-cross-task-relationships/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-a3d34d2a90b174f4">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:cwm" data-paper-title="Counteracting Duration Bias in Video Recommendation via Counterfactual Watch Time" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Learning signals, multitask learning, and feedback bias</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-cwm-65e93cb4" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-26b7e8adddd68f37">How does CWM&#x27;s potential watch benefit under common duration differ from observed watched seconds?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Acwm">Counteracting Duration Bias in Video Recommendation via Counterfactual Watch Time</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Kuaishou Technology / Renmin University of China</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Observed seconds mix preference, duration constraints, and content-type relationships. A common duration intervention compares potential outcomes at equal opportunity, reducing inherent long-video advantage. It is unobserved and requires modeling and identification assumptions.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Completing a 15-second clip versus watching two minutes of a longer clip cannot determine preference from seconds alone.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.07932">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2406.07932-cwm/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-26b7e8adddd68f37">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:cwm" data-paper-title="Counteracting Duration Bias in Video Recommendation via Counterfactual Watch Time" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Learning signals, multitask learning, and feedback bias</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-08cd76fbd0f6979a">Why might counterfactual watch-time scoring better capture preferences than raw watched seconds?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Acwm">Counteracting Duration Bias in Video Recommendation via Counterfactual Watch Time</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Kuaishou Technology / Renmin University of China</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Raw seconds combine attraction with the viewing opportunity allowed by duration. CWM estimates potential watch benefit under a common duration intervention. This depends on counterfactual assumptions, is not just dividing by duration, and local proxies do not establish that actual duration or exposure confounding was removed.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Completing a 20-second clip and abandoning a long clip after 30 seconds may imply a different preference under equal viewing opportunity.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.07932">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2406.07932-cwm/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-08cd76fbd0f6979a">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:cwm" data-paper-title="Counteracting Duration Bias in Video Recommendation via Counterfactual Watch Time" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Learning signals, multitask learning, and feedback bias</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-5537f98a3b8a194f">How do CWM and completion-rate ranking differ in their assumptions about duration?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Acwm">Counteracting Duration Bias in Video Recommendation via Counterfactual Watch Time</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Kuaishou Technology / Renmin University of China</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Completion rate is an observed ratio and can favor short content; it has no explicit counterfactual. CWM estimates a potential outcome under common duration to separate preferences and duration effects. Bias differs, and misspecification can prevent the causal objective from helping.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A three-second ad is easy to complete, unlike a long tutorial. CWM instead asks which would offer more value at equal duration.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.07932">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2406.07932-cwm/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-5537f98a3b8a194f">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:cwm" data-paper-title="Counteracting Duration Bias in Video Recommendation via Counterfactual Watch Time" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Learning signals, multitask learning, and feedback bias</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-1a473e83d1d8b5a0">How should training and prediction duration differ for CWM&#x27;s `do(D=d0)`?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Acwm">Counteracting Duration Bias in Video Recommendation via Counterfactual Watch Time</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Kuaishou Technology / Renmin University of China</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Fit the duration mechanism using observed D; for prediction comparisons fix d0 and output the defined potential quantity and bias term. Using each item&#x27;s original duration is not a common intervention. Local movie proxies do not measure real short-video potential watch benefit.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Set the same d0 for a 30-second clip and a five-minute clip; setting 30 and 300 reintroduces the original difference.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.07932">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2406.07932-cwm/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-1a473e83d1d8b5a0">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:dadf" data-paper-title="DADF: A Distribution-Aware Debiasing Framework for Watch-Time Regression in Recommender Systems" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="basics" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Learning signals, multitask learning, and feedback bias</a></p>
<span id="paper-recommendation-dadf-696311de" class="ar-learning-paper-anchor"></span>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Basics</p>
<h2 id="qa-4ed21b3ed0463b49">Why treat DADF&#x27;s mature predictor as a baseline and learn a relative correction?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Adadf">DADF: A Distribution-Aware Debiasing Framework for Watch-Time Regression in Recommender Systems</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Kuaishou Technology</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>The predictor already captures stable relationships. A separate factor focuses on conditional systematic errors with the same scalar interface and less risk than full retraining. Near-zero or badly misspecified predictions are harder to correct, and factors cannot recreate missing information.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>Correct a 10% long-video underestimate without discarding every learned user-content relationship.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.17863">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2605.17863-dadf/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-4ed21b3ed0463b49">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:dadf" data-paper-title="DADF: A Distribution-Aware Debiasing Framework for Watch-Time Regression in Recommender Systems" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="mechanism" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Learning signals, multitask learning, and feedback bias</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Core mechanism</p>
<h2 id="qa-3c6b5e2b06c5bf58">Why does DADF freeze the mature first-stage model and learn a multiplicative factor?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Adadf">DADF: A Distribution-Aware Debiasing Framework for Watch-Time Regression in Recommender Systems</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Kuaishou Technology</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Retraining can damage established capabilities or interfaces. Distribution-conditioned proportional residuals adapt to inputs and base predictions while preserving the scalar output. Tiny predictions can destabilize ratios, so check denominator protection and conditional distribution calibration.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>If two groups each start at 10 seconds but one is overestimated and one underestimated, learn distinct factors instead of adding five seconds everywhere.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.17863">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2605.17863-dadf/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-3c6b5e2b06c5bf58">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:dadf" data-paper-title="DADF: A Distribution-Aware Debiasing Framework for Watch-Time Regression in Recommender Systems" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="comparison" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Learning signals, multitask learning, and feedback bias</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Method comparison</p>
<h2 id="qa-03765f3ee2f1d912">How do DADF&#x27;s multiplicative and additive residuals affect scale differently?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Adadf">DADF: A Distribution-Aware Debiasing Framework for Watch-Time Regression in Recommender Systems</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Kuaishou Technology</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Multiplication expresses proportional error and therefore larger absolute adjustments for large predictions; addition expresses fixed-unit error. Choose based on error structure. The local ranking was unchanged, so calibration changes are not automatic recommendation gains.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-example"><strong>Illustrative example: </strong>A 10% underestimate at 10 and 100 seconds suits multiplication; a consistent five-second error suits addition. A global multiplier preserves ranking.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-sources">Sections in the Chinese source: 背景与主要改动, 核心公式. The example illustrates the mechanism.</p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.17863">Original paper</a> · <a href="../../../../../reproductions/2605.17863-dadf/README-en/">Implementation write-up</a> · <a href="#qa-03765f3ee2f1d912">Question link</a></p>
</details>
</article>
<article class="ar-learning-card ar-learning-qa" data-learning-card data-identity="recommendation:dadf" data-paper-title="DADF: A Distribution-Aware Debiasing Framework for Watch-Time Regression in Recommender Systems" data-learning-pending="false" data-level="implementation" data-domain="recommendation" data-theme="recommendation" data-topic="recommendation/feedback-multitask-causality">
<p class="ar-learning-card__domain"><a href="./">Search, ads, and recommendation / Learning signals, multitask learning, and feedback bias</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-level">Implementation details</p>
<h2 id="qa-ea006a6d3351f5f2">Why check small denominators in DADF&#x27;s `y/max(y0,ε)` even with frozen y0?</h2>
<p class="ar-learning-paper"><a href="../../../all/?paper=recommendation%3Adadf">DADF: A Distribution-Aware Debiasing Framework for Watch-Time Regression in Recommender Systems</a></p>
<p class="ar-learning-card__meta">Question added: 2026-10-27 · Kuaishou Technology</p>
<details class="ar-learning-answer"><summary>Show answer and example</summary>
<p><strong>Answer: </strong>Freezing stabilizes supervision but tiny predictions can produce huge noisy ratios.
